Week 16 evidence receipt — Farkle / Machine Learning fun week

Purpose

A light, honest record of the Wednesday/Friday Farkle experiment (lessons/10-farkle-ml.md) — proof you played, ran the experiment, and can reason about what it showed. This is the fun week; keep it short.

Not a Reasoning Odyssey checkpoint or gate. No Odyssey gate is due this week (see assignments/odyssey_gates/week-16.md). This receipt is a separate, small, applied-session artifact — see docs/grading-model.md's participation/reflection evidence categories for where this kind of weekly artifact fits; no new grading category or point value is introduced by this file (see that document's Open decisions if a specific weight still needs to be assigned).

Do

Fill out every section below in your own words. Two to four sentences per numbered item is normal — this is not a report.

1. Your human strategy

State the rule you used before seeing the machine, in one plain sentence (e.g., "bank once I hit 400, unless I'm close to winning, then I bank sooner").

2. What you ran

  • Command(s) you ran, with the --seed and --games/--turns values you used.
  • Number of simulated games/turns behind your evidence.

3. Evidence: strategy vs. strategy, or before vs. after learning

Paste (or summarize in a small table) the actual printed comparison — win rate, average score, and Farkle rate for both sides.

4. Interpretation questions (answer at least 3 of the 5 from the lesson)

Use lessons/10-farkle-ml.md §6. Quote or paraphrase the specific question you're answering.

5. One surprise

Something in the numbers you did not expect.

6. One limitation

Something the machine's table does not account for (hint: what's in the state dictionary, and what isn't).

Support and integrity

Use the supplied simulator (lessons/code/farkle/) — you are not expected to write a Farkle engine from scratch this week. AI tools may help you interpret output or debug a command, same as any other week; verify and explain any claim in your own words, and credit help used, per this course's standing AI-use policy.

description:
Student Activity — AI I Week 16: Reflect and Improve

Big Question: How has my thinking changed because of this course?

This is the capstone. You are not learning a new AI technique today. You are assembling evidence of how the first 15 lenses changed the way you think and work.

A Single Thread: Your Portfolio

Imagine that you will use AI tomorrow in a course you have not taken. Before trusting its first answer, what would you do?

Write one action. It might involve defining the task, checking assumptions, asking for critique, verifying a claim, revising the result, or measuring whether it meets the goal.

Now use your own Weeks 1–15 portfolio to show how you learned that habit.

Step 1: Find the Change

Choose:

  • one early artifact that shows how you started;
  • one later artifact that shows a stronger practice; and
  • one critique, verification, or revision that connects them.

Write:

Earlier, I ____. Now, I ___. The change happened or became visible when _____.

Be specific. “I got better at AI” is not enough.

Step 2: Complete the Evidence Map

Use these artifacts as possible evidence:

  • Problem Definition Card;
  • Context Comparison Sheet;
  • Plan-first Workflow;
  • Decomposed Task Pipeline;
  • Model Comparison Table;
  • Prompt Makeover;
  • RAG On/Off Comparison;
  • Assumptions and Tradeoffs Analysis;
  • Audience Transformation Outputs;
  • Debate Club Critique Record;
  • Claim Verification Table;
  • Before/After Revision;
  • Decision Matrix;
  • Reusable Prompt Chain;
  • Rubric Evaluation.

You do not need to use every artifact. Select the evidence that actually supports your claims.

Step 3: Assemble Eight Sections

Your final portfolio must contain:

  1. My AI thinking philosophy
  2. My best prompt and why it works
  3. My biggest AI mistake and what I learned
  4. My best critique example
  5. My best verification example
  6. My best revision example
  7. My reusable AI workflow
  8. My plan for using AI responsibly in future courses or work

For each section, reference the artifact or artifacts you used. Explain what the evidence shows; do not merely list a filename or week.

Step 4: Write Your Reusable Workflow

Write a short sequence that you could repeat:

  1. define the task and success condition;
  2. provide relevant context and identify what is missing;
  3. plan or ask for an approach before producing;
  4. critique assumptions, reasoning, or output;
  5. verify important claims and behavior;
  6. revise;
  7. evaluate whether the result meets the goal and course rules.

Adapt the sequence to your own practice. A workflow should be repeatable and proportionate, not unnecessarily long.

Step 5: Plan Forward

Complete:

In a future course or workplace, I will use this workflow when ____. I will use AI responsibly by ___. I will still personally check _____.

You do not need to name a personal employer, project, health matter, family situation, or other private detail.

Optional AI Coach

If you have access to a course-approved tool, you may use it only as a reflection coach:

I am assembling a final portfolio from my own course artifacts. Ask me questions that help me identify one specific change in my thinking, the evidence for that change, and how I will use the habit in future work. Do not invent evidence, write my reflection for me, or make claims about artifacts you have not seen.

Do not enter private information or anything your course policy prohibits. Check every suggestion against your own artifacts. You write the final portfolio.

If you do not use a tool, use the questions and template in this activity. That is the complete alternative.

Exit Ticket

Complete this sentence:

Because of this course, I now ______ before I trust or use AI output.

Your unofficial transcript is the "receipt" of your college journey so far:

Submit two files in Canvas:

  2. Quick reflection (short write-up) — a short reflection as PDF or Markdown. File name: {COURSE}_A01_TranscriptReflection_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf (or .md)

A03 — Personal semester-by-semester degree plan

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, by end of day.

Why we're doing this

This assignment helps you build a realistic plan for graduation. You'll use your unofficial transcript (A01), progress report (A02), and your institution's catalog/schedule to map out your remaining semesters and confirm prerequisites and course availability. Connect the dots and land on the semester you actually expect to graduate.

This is a planning tool you should keep and update all semester — bring it to advising appointments. (Tape it to your wall for the days you want to give up.)

What you will submit

Upload one PDF, exported from a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets).

File naming: {COURSE}_A03_DegreePlan_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A03_DegreePlan_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Requirements (what must be in your spreadsheet)

1) Title + basics (top of page) — your name; major (and minor if applicable); option (if applicable); your expected graduation semester (e.g. "Spring 2028").

2) Semester-by-semester plan (the main table) — list every semester from now until graduation. For each planned course: course prefix/number, course name, credits, and optional notes ("needs prereq," "only offered fall," etc.). For each semester: total credits.

3) Prerequisites + reality check — show evidence you checked your institution's course catalog/schedule offerings, your progress report (what remains), and your unofficial transcript (what's completed). This can be a short "checked list," notes in a dedicated column, or a small "Verification" box.

4) Two scenarios (minimum) — e.g. Scenario A (~12 credits/semester) and Scenario B (~18 credits/semester with summer classes). For each, show the expected graduation term and what changes between the two plans.

5) Advising notes / questions — a short list (minimum 2 items) of questions or notes for an advisor, e.g. "Is Course X offered every spring?" or "Do I need an elective in category Y?"

Step-by-step instructions (how to build it)

  1. Open Excel or Google Sheets.
  2. Create a sheet named "Degree Plan."
  3. Add your title + graduation target at the top.
  4. Build your main table (suggested columns: Semester | Course # | Course Name | Credits | Notes).
  5. Add semester totals (a SUM at the bottom of each semester block works).
  6. Duplicate the sheet (or add a second section) for Scenario B.
  7. Export as PDF (Excel: File → Export → Create PDF; Google Sheets: File → Download → PDF).

Late / revision notes

If something doesn't make sense (missing prereqs, unsure offering), mark it clearly as a question — don't guess silently. Planning is allowed to be imperfect; hiding uncertainty is not.

Need help?

If anything looks unexpected in your progress report or transcript, message the instructor.

description:
A08 — Degree Reflection

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, alongside A01–A03, by end of day.

Why this is a separate assignment

A01–A03 prove you can find the data (transcript, progress report, degree plan) and read it correctly. This assignment is graded on whether you actually thought about what that data means for you. It is deliberately not a paragraph folded into the end of A01 or A03 — it is its own assignment, with its own points, and every question below is its own graded line. Reflection is the part of Semester Kick Off Week that's easiest to skip when it's buried as an afterthought in another assignment's write-up. Making it separate, numbered, and individually pointed is this course's way of saying: this isn't filler, it's the point of the week.

Where this structure comes from

The questions below borrow their shape from two goal-setting/productivity frameworks — Michael Hyatt's Your Best Year Ever (naming what excites you and what you're afraid of, then converting both into a real plan) and Free to Focus (sorting what's ahead of you instead of just reacting to it). You don't need to have read either book. The questions stand on their own; the framework just explains why they're shaped the way they are, in case you're curious.

Using an LLM here (encouraged, with one boundary)

Use an LLM to think wider, not to think for you:

  • Stuck on Q5 (three mitigating ideas)? Ask an LLM to brainstorm eight or ten, then pick your own three and say why.
  • Not sure what a class or requirement actually involves? Ask an LLM to summarize a syllabus or department page you paste in, then react to that summary in your own words.

The choice, the reasoning, and the plan have to be yours. An LLM that writes your answer for you defeats the purpose — this assignment exists to find out what you think about your own degree, not what a model guesses a good student would say. Grading can tell the difference (see rubrics/A08_rubric.md): a generic, could-be-anyone answer scores lower than a specific one, regardless of how polished the writing is.

What you will submit

A Canvas text entry (no file upload) with nine numbered answers, answered individually — don't merge them into one essay. Numbering them separately is what makes each one gradable, and visible, on its own.

Part 1 — What excites you

Q1. Which class or requirement still ahead of you excites you the most? Name it specifically — a course number and title if it's a single course, or the exact requirement category (e.g. "the lab science requirement," not "gen eds" or "a science class") if it isn't tied to one course yet — and say why. (2 pts)

Q2. What's the best use of your time between now and when you take it, so you actually get the most out of it — not just survive it? (2 pts)

Q3. How does that class connect to the career you're aiming for? Name the specific job-market skill or requirement it builds toward — be concrete, not "it'll help in general." (2 pts)

Part 2 — What worries you

Q4. What are you afraid of for your degree — a specific class, requirement, or milestone? Name it. ("Math" is not an answer; "Calculus II, because I barely passed Calculus I" is.) (2 pts)

Q5. List three mitigating ideas for that situation — three genuinely different approaches, not three phrasings of the same one idea. (3 pts — 1 per distinct, real idea)

A09 — Career Reflection

Due: Friday of Semester Kick Off Week, alongside A04–A06, by 4:00 PM.

Why this is a separate assignment

A04–A06 prove you can build a resume, name a real target job, and compare your skills against it. This assignment is graded on whether you actually thought about what that target job means for you — what you're looking forward to, and what genuinely worries you about it. Like A08, it's separate from A04–A06 on purpose, with its own points on its own numbered lines, so there's no ambiguity about whether reflection is optional. It isn't.

Where this structure comes from

Part 1 borrows from the idea of a "Desire Zone" (from Michael Hyatt's Free to Focus) — the parts of a job where you're both good at the work and genuinely want to do it, as opposed to work you can do but dread. Part 2 borrows from the same book's sorting habit — name the hard thing honestly, then find a real way to handle it, rather than hoping it resolves itself. Part 3 borrows from Your Best Year Ever's "find your why." You don't need to have read either book.

Using an LLM here (encouraged, with one boundary)

Use an LLM to research and widen your options — summarize a real job posting, generate more mitigating strategies than you'd think of alone, or role-play what a day in that job might actually look like. Then decide for yourself and write the decision in your own words. An LLM writing the final answer for you defeats the point — grading rewards specific, personal reasoning over generic polish (see rubrics/A09_rubric.md).

What you will submit

A Canvas text entry (no file upload) with nine numbered answers, answered individually — don't merge them into one essay.

Part 1 — What you're eager for (the Desire Zone)

Q1. From your A05 dream job, what specific part of the work are you most eager for? Name the actual task or responsibility (not just "the job" or "the money"), and say why. (2 pts)

Q2. Which class, project, or experience — name it specifically — best prepares you for that part? (2 pts)

Q3. What's the best use of your time this semester to build toward it? (2 pts)

Part 2 — What will be hardest

Q4. What part of this career do you expect to be the most difficult? Name a specific skill, task type, or environment — not "it'll be hard." (2 pts)

Q5. List three mitigating strategies for that difficulty — a course, a habit, a person to ask, a project to attempt. Three genuinely different approaches, not one idea said three ways. (3 pts — 1 per distinct, real idea)

Q6. Which is your favorite — the one you'll actually act on? Why that one, and not the others? (2 pts)

Q7. Which class, skill, or experience between now and graduation most directly addresses this difficulty? (2 pts)

Q8. What's your concrete next step, and by when? (2 pts)

Part 3 — Why it matters

Q9. How does this career direction align with your values? Name one place of real fit, and one place of real tension — and how you'd resolve the tension. (3 pts)

Total: 20 points

Need help?

If you're between two target jobs, pick the one you named in A05 and answer for that one — you can revisit the other later.

See rubrics/A09_rubric.md for grading.

A10 (Optional / Bonus) — Success Foundations Reflection

This assignment is optional bonus work, not required. It has no fixed due date tied to A04–A06/A09 or the rest of Kickoff Week's Friday load — complete it whenever you like during the semester. (Earlier, this was briefly assigned as required, graded work due the same day as A04-A06/A09; Jeremy reversed that call the same day — see semester_kickoff_week/success_foundations_supplemental/README.md for the history.)

Why this is here

Building a resume (A04), naming a real target job (A05), and comparing your skills against it (A06) all raise the same question in the background: how do you actually get from where you are now to that job? This assignment lets you step back and think about that, using the mastery framework from the companion reading, success_foundations_reading.md (drawn from How Learning Works, Ch. 3). Complete the reading first; answer in your own words, not copied sentences from it.

What you will submit

A Canvas text entry (no file upload) with four numbered answers, 2–4 sentences each unless a question says otherwise.

Questions

  1. Recall/comprehension. The reading identifies three things learners need to develop mastery: component skills, integration/fluency of those skills, and knowing when/where to apply them. Pick one of the three and explain, in your own words, what it means and why it's not enough on its own. (3 pts)

  2. Recall/comprehension. What does the reading mean by "cognitive load," and what are the three types it names (intrinsic, extraneous, germane)? (2 pts)

Which of those component skills is currently your weakest, and how do you know? (3 pts)

  4. Application. The reading describes an "expert blind spot," where experienced people underestimate how much a novice needs explained. Describe one time you experienced this — either as the novice confused by an expert's shortcut, or as someone further along who caught yourself assuming something was obvious. (2 pts)

Total: 10 points (bonus)

description:
Student Activity — AI I Week 2: Gather Context

Big Question: What information would make the AI answer dramatically better?

Last week you wrote down what you'd have to ask before a vague request was worth acting on. This week you supply it — and you decide how much of it is actually worth sending.

You don't need any prior AI experience for this activity, and you do not need to be able to write the program yourself. Your job is to specify it. You can work alone or with a partner.

The Scenario

The student who runs the campus coffee cart put a note on the department bulletin board:

"Can someone write me a program that calculates the total?"

That's the whole request. Your instructor will show an instructor-authored illustration: five clean lines that add up three arbitrary numbers and print The total is: 30. No bugs. No coffee. A live AI response can differ, but it still needs the missing information before it can address the coffee-cart task.

Step 1: Write Three Versions of the Same Request

Same task, three levels of context.

Version 1 — no context. This one's done for you. It's the request as posted:

"Write a Python program that calculates the total."

Version 2 — some context. Add what the task actually is. Someone types in a price and a number of drinks; the program prints a total. Write the request out in one or two sentences.

Version 3 — rich context. Add the rest. Work through these — most people skip at least two:

  • Audience. Who runs this program? And who wrote it — what has that person actually learned so far?
  • Background. What does the AI need to know about coffee that it can't get from the word "total"? (Start here: how many drinks can someone buy? Can it be 2.5?)
  • Constraints. How long should it be? Is anything off-limits?
  • Format. What should the output look like? Would you hand a customer a price that reads 14.549999999999999?

Step 2: Say What Each Version Still Has to Guess

Before you run anything, write down — for each of your three versions — what does the AI still have to guess?

This is the actual work of the activity. "Version 3 is better" is not an answer. "Version 2 doesn't say whether the number of drinks is a whole number, so the AI has to pick" is.

Step 3: Compare

If you have access to an AI tool:

  1. Submit Version 1. Save the response.
  2. Submit Version 2. Save it.
  3. Submit Version 3. Save it.
  4. Compare all three: for each one, what did the AI have to guess, and would this actually work for the coffee cart?

If you don't have tool access:

Your instructor will show three prepared programs, one for each version, and the class compares them the same way. (These are examples your instructor wrote to show the contrast, not real AI output — but the comparison works identically, and this is not a lesser version of the activity.)

Privacy reminder: The coffee cart is made up. Keep it that way — never paste real names, real contact information, real business details, or any private, protected, or confidential information into an AI system.

Step 4: The Test That Matters

Add these four sentences to your Version 3:

"The coffee cart has been running since 2019. It's usually busiest between classes. My favorite drink is the lavender latte. The cart is painted teal."

Every one of them is true in this fictional scenario. Every one is about the coffee cart. Which of them changes the program requirements? A live AI may still change wording or code for unrelated reasons; judge whether it changed anything that matters to the task.

If the answer surprises you, that's this week:

More context is not always better. Relevant context is better.

There's one test, and it isn't "is this true?" or "is this related?" It's: does it change the answer?

Step 5: Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Fill out your own Context Comparison Sheet using what you produced in Steps 1–4. If you worked with a partner, discuss together but complete your own sheet. Save it with your Problem Definition Card from last week — together they're one continuous piece of thinking, and you'll want both at the end of the course.

The last line of the Sheet is the one worth slowing down for: one true thing you deliberately left out, and why it wouldn't have helped. Anyone can add information. Knowing what to leave out is the harder half, and it's the difference between a good request and a long one.

Exit Ticket

Before you leave: in one sentence, what's the difference between context that changes the answer and detail that just makes the request longer?
name: Monday Moment Activity — week_02_gather_context

rubric.long_description: One Context Comparison Sheet (three prompt versions plus reflection), assessed on whether the student identifies useful context, not just more context. Score only from this 0-10 point scale -- never use the qualitative labels (Incomplete/Revise/Check/Check-plus) alone. 0 points (Incomplete): not submitted, or too blank to read. 1-5 points (Revise): submitted, but fails at least one Check criterion below. 6-8 points (Check), all three required: (a) the three versions are genuinely distinct with Version 2 a real middle step; (b) Versions 1 and 2 each name something specific and plausible the AI had to guess; (c) the most-important-context answer names one specific piece of context and the specific thing it changed. 9-10 points (Check-plus), everything in Check plus both: (a) the left-out-on-purpose answer names a detail that is genuinely true but irrelevant, with a reason tied to whether it changes the answer (not just because it's uninteresting); (b) the sheet is internally consistent (the piece named as most important actually appears where the student says it does; the left-out detail really is irrelevant).

description:
Student Activity — AI I Week 3: Plan the Work

Big Question: Why should we ask AI to plan before we ask it to produce?

Last week you chose context that actually mattered and named what was still unknown. This week, use those facts before anyone drafts. Your job is to make the route visible—not to have AI write your CS1 work.

Start With Your Week 2 Handoff

Open your Context Comparison Sheet. Copy one context-selected task, one useful fact, and one consequential gap or assumption into your Plan-first Workflow. That real task is your default planning input.

If your task has a decision, use it for your own plan. If it does not, plan the whole route: settle needed information, name a real dependency, choose a task-appropriate checkpoint, and state what the eventual draft should do. If Week 2 ended with no open gap, carry forward one important gap you already settled or one assumption the plan still needs to check; do not invent a problem. The shared study-room scenario below is a complete common model for the CS1 branching connection and your fallback if you do not have the Week 2 sheet.

Shared CS1 Scenario

The campus library wants a tiny reminder program for a study room. A user enters an integer number of minutes remaining in a reservation. Expected valid values are 0 or greater. We trace -1 as an invalid test value and route it to “ended” only to keep this Week 3 condition-order example small. Production-quality input handling might reject the value and ask again; that later design is not part of this lesson.

The program should say:

Minutes remaining Message
0 or less Your reservation has ended.
1 through 10 Wrap up soon.
more than 10 Your room is still available.

This scenario is fictional. Do not use real names, reservation records, or private information in an AI tool.

Step 1: Start With What You Know

Write these on your Plan-first Workflow for your own carried-forward task. Use the study-room answers only if you are using the shared scenario:

  • One useful fact from last week's kind of work: the input is an integer number of minutes.
  • One gap that must be settled before drafting: does 0 mean ended or ending soon? For this task, it means ended.

Step 2: Plan Before Any Draft

Complete all six parts of your Workflow:

  1. objective;
  2. ordered stages;
  3. needed information;
  4. decision points or dependencies;
  5. risks; and
  6. quality checkpoints.

For a task with a decision, include: make a decision table, trace boundary values, and only then draft a branching chain. The shared CS1 scenario must use those stages. For a non-branching task, use another concrete pre-draft checkpoint, such as a hand calculation, required-information check, or exact-output check. A plan tells the route. It does not list separate modules, jobs, or interfaces—that is next week's question.

Step 3: Critique and Revise

For the shared case, check your plan with these values: -1, 0, 1, 10, and 11. For your own carried-forward task, choose comparable boundary values, decisions, calculations, requirements, or checkpoints.

Ask: “Will my route send each value to the intended message? Is a broad condition placed before a narrower one?” For a non-branching task, ask whether the route settles the needed facts and checks the exact result before drafting. Record one risk or assumption, then make one visible improvement to the route—an order, checkpoint, needed fact, or explanation. Revision shows what inspection taught you; it does not mean the first plan was a failure.

Step 4: Write Only After Revision

Complete the Write From the Revised Plan field. For a branching task, write one final plain-language decision rule. For the study-room example: “Check whether the reservation has ended before checking whether it is ending soon.” For a non-branching task, write a plain-language instruction or next-draft statement that follows from the route—for example, “Calculate the subtotal and tax, then check the exact two-decimal output before drafting the program.” In the associated CS1 work, you may use your own plan to write your own code. Do not copy code from an AI tool.

Step 5: Compare Two Workflows

If you have a course-approved AI tool, try both workflows:

  1. Use the instructor’s prepared direct-work draft as the immediate-write comparison. It is instructor-authored, not AI output.
  2. Ask a tool for a plan only: stages, needed information, risks, and quality checks. Ask it to critique the plan without writing code.

For the shared case, ask which workflow made the 0-minute decision visible sooner. For your own carried-forward task, name the key decision, dependency, assumption, or checkpoint that planning made visible sooner.

If you do not have a tool, use the instructor’s prepared direct-work draft and plan-first comparison. It gives you the same evidence and is not a lesser activity.

Step 6: Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Complete your own Plan-first Workflow, including its final plain-language write. Save it with your Problem Definition Card and Context Comparison Sheet. Your artifact is the plan, its revision, and the statement produced from that revised route—not a finished program.

Exit Ticket

In one sentence: what did the plan let you notice before a draft could hide it?
name: Monday Moment Activity — week_03_plan_the_work

rubric.long_description: One Plan-first Workflow artifact for a decision or non-branching task, assessed on whether the student planned and checked before drafting, not after. Score only from this 0-10 point scale -- never use the qualitative labels alone. 0 points (Incomplete): no usable workflow submitted. 1-5 points (Revise): a usable workflow that fails at least one Check criterion below -- including an ordered function/owner/interface inventory offered instead of a whole-task pre-draft route. 6-8 points (Check): a task-specific objective; an ordered whole-task route with a concrete checkpoint before drafting (a decision task uses a decision table and boundary trace); a needed fact; a concrete decision or dependency; a risk; a critique with a visible route improvement; and a final plain-language write that follows from the revision. 9-10 points (Check-plus): everything in Check, plus a specific risk or assumption, a critique that identifies a plausible route defect, and a revision that clearly improves an order, decision, checkpoint, or needed information and explains why it is safer or clearer.

description:
Student Activity — AI I Week 4: Decompose the Task

Delivery note: Monday is Labor Day, so this activity begins with a short introduction before Wednesday’s Professional Minds conversation. Complete the pipeline as light homework or carry-forward work.

Big Question: How do we split large AI tasks into smaller, safer, more useful pieces?

The Scenario

A campus team wants a proposal for a campus food pantry app. The app may help people learn pantry hours, understand available services, and plan a visit.

This is a fictional scenario. Do not add real names, student records, health information, food-access information, or other private details.

Step 1: See the Large Request

The large request is:

Create a proposal for a campus food pantry app. Identify users, define goals, gather requirements, list features, identify risks, build a timeline, draft the proposal, critique it, and revise it.

Before splitting it up, answer:

  • What decisions are hidden inside this request?
  • What could go wrong if the proposal were drafted immediately?

Step 2: Build the Pipeline

Use the portfolio artifact to create at least three ordered stages. The complete source example includes these possible stages:

  1. identify stakeholders;
  2. define goals;
  3. gather requirements;
  4. list features;
  5. identify risks;
  6. build a timeline;
  7. draft the proposal;
  8. critique the proposal;
  9. revise the proposal.

You may combine stages when you can explain why one boundary is enough. You may add a stage when it catches an important uncertainty.

For every stage, record:

Big Question: How do we ground AI output in trusted information?

The Scenario

  2. with a short source excerpt.

Your goal is to notice what the source changes and whether the answer stays within the evidence.

Source Excerpt

A function is a named, reusable piece of a program. Parameters allow a function to receive information. A return value sends a result back to the part of the program that called the function. A returned result can be stored, printed, or used in another calculation. A function may perform an action without returning a value.

What RAG Means

RAG means retrieval-augmented generation.

In plain language, it means giving an AI relevant source material before asking it to answer. The source may be a lesson, syllabus, public article, policy, or dataset.

Big Question: How do we know whether an AI answer is trustworthy?

A polished answer can still contain false claims. Your job is to separate claims from style, identify the evidence needed, and record what the evidence actually shows.

The Scenario

A library is considering a small Room Reservation Records program. Read this confident answer:

The Room Reservation Records program is ready for delivery. It stores each reservation in a dictionary, so every reservation is preserved and can be looked up quickly. The sample data contains two reservations for Ari, and the program will keep both of them. Since the program works on the sample data, it will also work for an empty list of reservations. The library should adopt this approach because dictionaries are the best choice for reservation systems. By next semester, most campus reservation systems will use this pattern.

This is a fictional scenario. Do not use real names, reservation records, or private information in an AI tool.

Claim Types

Use the type that best fits each claim:

  • Factual: describes information that can usually be checked against a reliable source or the given data.
  • Programmatic: describes what code does. Check it by tracing or running relevant inputs.
  • Predictive: describes what may happen in the future. Current evidence can support or weaken it, but cannot confirm the future today.
  • Normative/design: says what should be chosen or done. Evidence can inform the judgment, but does not settle the value choice by itself.

These claim types are not equally easy to verify.

Evidence for the Scenario

scores = {}
for name, score in records:
    scores[name] = score

print(scores)

records = [("Ari", 80), ("Bo", 90), ("Ari", 95)]

The output is:

{'Ari': 95, 'Bo': 90}

For:

the output is:

{}

A dictionary maps each key to one current value. Assigning a new value to an existing key replaces the previous value for that key.

Do not mark a claim verified because it sounds polished. “Uncertain” is a valid result when the available evidence cannot settle the claim.

Complete this after reading readings/week_15_fri_evaluating_ai_harms.md in full. Answer in your own words — do not copy sentences from the reading. Each answer should be 2-4 sentences unless the question says otherwise.

  1. Recall/comprehension. Explain the difference between local and global factual consistency, using the reading's own examples. Why is a global-consistency claim generally harder to verify?

  4. Application. The reading describes RealToxicityPrompts as prompts specifically engineered to bait toxic completions, not random prompts. Explain why testing a model's behavior under this kind of provocation is a different (and necessary) check than testing its average, everyday behavior.

This assignment is derived from readings/week_15_fri_evaluating_ai_harms.md, itself drawn from AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models by Chip Huyen, Chapter 4, "Evaluate AI Systems." description:
Paired programming and explanation

Purpose

Practice explaining your reasoning out loud and reading someone else's code, not just producing your own. Pair programming is the Wednesday active work in this course's weekly rhythm (docs/course-ethos.md).

Do

  1. Work with a partner on the current week's problems (the same problems as assignments/A1-weekly-coding-practice.md, done together instead of solo). Take turns driving (typing) and navigating (reading, catching mistakes, asking questions); switch roles at least once per session.
  2. If you share one repository, each partner commits their own work. Your pair's git log must show a lines-of-code split no more lopsided than 80/20 — if one partner is consistently driving, that's a problem to fix before it's a grading problem.
  3. Record, in your own words: the problem, your approach, what changed in the code, how you tested it, and specifically what you contributed versus your partner.
  4. Note any outside help or AI/resource use — whose idea it was, and how you verified it.
  5. Present your progress to your partner or the class when scheduled.

What you submit: the paired-programming report

This is your own individual report, even if the code is shared — it's graded on your documented contribution, not the pair's combined output (docs/grading-model.md, 5% of the course grade). Include:

  • The problem and your approach, briefly.
  • What you personally wrote, fixed, or figured out (be specific — "helped with the loop" is not specific; "wrote the sentinel condition after our first version looped forever" is).
  • A pointer to the commit(s) or lines that back that claim up.
  • Anything you learned from watching or being corrected by your partner.

Separately: the Friday feedback report

If your section does Friday show-and-tell peer feedback, that's graded separately as its own 5% category — see assignments/A4-show-and-tell-reflection.md and docs/grading-model.md. Don't fold it into this report.

Support and integrity

If schedule or enrollment makes pairing impractical some weeks, this format may be dropped for that week — check with your instructor rather than skipping silently. Ask questions in class or office hours if you're unsure how to document a contribution split fairly.
